rv.q: The Sugar Wife is a masterpiece of a play, a kaleidoscope of humanity’s complex relationships – with each other, with hope and hypocrisy, and with morality in an immoral world.
The genius of this play and production is that it refuses to provide any clarity; indeed, it willfully denies us catharsis.
The Sugar Wife reminds us of the bitter truth that many of us are both complicit and victimized in global systems of exploitation.
At two and a half hours, that is something it needs at times.
Despite skillful direction and scenic design by Kevin Hagan, and truly great costumes by Rachel Lambert, it's a slow grind through what is essentially a melodrama, to get to the bottom of it all.

You’ll not find a better vehicle for accomplishing this uncommon feat than snagging a ticket to The Artistic Home’s marvelous new production of The Sugar Wife ; now at the beginning of its run at Theater Wit on Belmont.
The Sugar Wife is a quietly powerful, affecting show that lingers long after the final bow.
This is a provocative and intellectually engaging examination of integrity and interpersonal relationships within the context of rigid social constraints and gender expectations of the 19 th century.
Elizabeth Kuti's play is very strong and The Artistic Home Company makes it one to see.
Supported by compelling performances and strong design elements, this production offers a reflective, if uneven, exploration of the human cost behind systems too often accepted at face value.

cn.t: Critics praise this slow-burning, intellectually engaging drama for its sharp wit and powerful exploration of morality, capitalism, and hypocrisy in 1850s Dublin, calling it a devastating and exhilarating theatrical highpoint.
